Drones: Helpful or
Harmful?
Today's Focus:
• Decoding the Task: Transitioning from rigid essay patterns to an engaging magazine tone.
• The 3S Formula: Crafting hook-driven introductions that draw readers in.
• Paragraph Development: Using Point → Why → Example → Impact to prove and elaborate.
Decoding the Task: We Are Magazine Editors, Not Essayists
WHO IS WRITING?
The Writer
You are the Editor of Tech and Life
Today, an IT magazine. Your
register must be informative yet
highly engaging and reader-
friendly.
WHY ARE WE WRITING?
The Purpose
Explain why drones are popular,
how they are useful, what problems
they cause, and how they may be
used in the future.
WHO IS READING?
The Audience
Magazine readers interested in
technology and daily life. You must
inform and engage them, not
lecture them with academic jargon.
What Makes an Article Engaging? The Hook Test
INTRODUCTION A (The Rigid Essayist)
Drones are becoming popular nowadays. They are
useful in many ways. However, they can also cause
problems. In the future, drones may become even more
common.
INTRODUCTION B (The Feature Journalist)
Look up, and you might just spot one.
Drones are no longer limited to military operations; they
are increasingly becoming part of our everyday lives.
From delivering packages to helping during
emergencies, these flying machines are changing the
way we live.
WHICH ONE WOULD YOU RATHER READ?
A Good Introduction must be: Interesting (Hook) + Relevant (Topic) + Clear (Roadmap)
Building Your Introduction: The 3S Formula
STEP 1
START
"Look up, and you might just spot one."
Grab the reader's attention with a punchy hook.
Make them curious, involved, and eager to
read on.
STEP 2
SET THE SCENE
"Drones are no longer limited to military
use; they are becoming part of our daily
lives."
Introduce the topic naturally in context. Explain
what the conversation is about without
sounding like a textbook.
STEP 3
SIGNPOST
"But why are they so popular, how are they
helping us, and what problems might they
bring?"
Turn the DSE task requirements into
conversational questions that act as a reader-
friendly roadmap.
KEY INSIGHT FOR HIGH MARKS:
Turn the dry task requirements into a reader-friendly roadmap. Good writing does not simply state what you will talk about; it gives the reader an
compelling reason to keep reading.
Structure of a Power-Packed Paragraph
POINT
MAIN ASSERTION ABOUT
USEFULNESS
Drones are increasingly popular because they are useful and convenient.
WHY?
THE RATIONAL EXPLANATION They can complete tasks more quickly and reach places that are difficult for people to access.
EXAMPLE
CONCRETE REAL-WORLD EVIDENCE For example, drones can deliver packages, monitor crops, and assist rescuers during emergencies.
IMPACT
THE BIG PICTURE SIGNIFICANCE As a result, drones are no longer simply high-tech gadgets; they are becoming practical tools in everyday life.
Don't Just List. Develop Your Ideas.
LEVEL 1
WEAK: Just Listing
"Drones can be used for delivery,
farming and rescue."
❌Merely lists nouns without describing action.
❌Left with no explanation of
how they help.
❌Reader is left asking: 'So
what?'
LEVEL 2
BETTER: Explaining
"Drones can deliver small packages
without being affected by traffic."
✔Adds visual detail.
✔Explains the concrete
advantage.
✔Reader can visualize the
speed.
LEVEL 3
BEST: Impact
"Drones can deliver small packages
without being affected by traffic, which
may make last-mile delivery faster and
more efficient."
🏆Integrates Example + Explanation.
🏆Shows long-term societal
significance.
🏆Sophisticated sentence
structure with relative clauses.
Your Turn: The 5-Minute Paragraph Challenge
PROMPT FOR GROUP WRITING:
Drones are becoming increasingly popular because ____________________.
In your groups of 4, collaborate to fill in the blank and develop a high-scoring paragraph using our structure. Ensure you cover all four elements:
1. POINT: Complete the topic sentence above.
2. WHY: Add one solid explanation sentence.
3. EXAMPLE: Provide a concrete, highly-visual real-world example.
4. IMPACT: Describe why this matters to society or the future.
ROLES IN GROUPS
1 Leader, 1 Timekeeper, 1 Writer, 1 Reporter
TIME LIMIT
5 Minutes for Writing + 2 Minutes for Peer Critique
SUCCESS CRITERIA
Clear Point? Explain Why? Clear Example?
Impact?
"Good writing is not
about using the most
difficult words.
It is about making your
ideas clear, relevant and
well developed for
your readers."
01
KNOW YOUR AUDIENCE
Before writing, ask WHO you are writing for and WHY. Match your register, tone, and
vocabulary to them (Informative & Engaging, not boring & academic).
02
ENGAGING INTRODUCTION
Ditch rigid structural templates. Follow the 3S Formula: Start with an attention-grabbing
Hook, Set the Scene naturally, and Signpost with reader questions.
03
DEVELOP YOUR IDEAS
Don't just list nouns or examples. Use Point → Why → Example → Impact. Build visual
descriptions, explain advantages, and connect to the bigger picture.
